definition: A vast region of northern Asia, usually defined by the Ural Mountains, the Arctic Ocean and the Pacific. It is a geographic and colonial category, not a single culture, and it contains many peoples, languages and ecologies.

A ritual specialist found among many Siberian peoples, called saman in Evenki and other Tungusic languages. The word entered European usage through Russian. Shamans heal, divine, guide souls and travel between worlds, and the practice remains alive today.

The frame drum used by many Siberian shamans, often described as a mount, boat or reindeer. Its beat carries the shaman between worlds, and its decoration may show spirits, landscapes or genealogies. It is a ritual instrument, not merely a musical one.

A creator-trickster of Kamchatka and Chukotka, known as Kutkinnaku among the Koryak, Kutkh among the Itelmen and by other names among the Chukchi. He makes land and light, shapes people, and behaves with comic greed and cunning rather than moral authority.

A sacred animal for many Siberian peoples, especially the Khanty and Mansi, who address him as an ancestor and honoured guest. The bear ceremony sings, feeds and sends him back to the sky, and the killing of a bear requires apology and respect.

The domesticated and wild deer of the northern tundra and taiga, central to Nenets, Evenki, Chukchi and other herding economies. Reindeer provide transport, clothing, meat and milk, and the herd's migrations shape the yearly life of the family.

The boreal forest belt of Siberia, dominated by larch, pine, spruce and birch. It is the home of many Evenki and other hunting and herding peoples, and it is a seasonal landscape of snow, bog and animal trails rather than an empty wilderness.

The treeless Arctic and sub-Arctic plain, where reindeer, mosses and lichens dominate and the ground may stay frozen for most of the year. Nenets, Chukchi and other herders move across it with their animals, following pasture and weather.

An Ob-Ugric people of western Siberia, living along the Ob and its tributaries. The Khanty are known for reindeer herding, hunting, fishing and the bear ceremony, and they maintain their language and rituals despite decades of Soviet pressure.

A Turkic-speaking people of the Lena valley and the Sakha Republic, also called Yakut. They are known for horse and cattle herding, the olonkho epic and the summer Yhyakh festival, and some Sakha communities also herd reindeer in the north.
